I wanted my own AI assistant. Not someone else's API, with someone else's rules and someone else's monthly bill. My own model, running on a computer I controlled, that I could plug into my coding tools like any other service.

The model is **Qwen3.8-27B-Uncensored-GGUF**, a 27-billion-parameter community release built on the Qwen3.8 architecture, with the usual safety fine-tuning stripped out. I run the Q5_K_M quantization, a 19.5 GB file. It has a hybrid state-space and attention architecture, a native context length of 262,144 tokens, and a built-in multi-token-prediction head (more on that shortly). Running my own copy meant no one else's content policy sat between me and my own tools.

A model that size needs a very specific, very expensive piece of hardware: a graphics card with a lot of memory, the kind normally bought by companies training the next big thing, not by one person for a side project. Buying one outright didn't make sense, so I rented one by the hour: a 32 GB NVIDIA V100, from [Vast.ai](https://vast.ai), a marketplace where people with spare GPU capacity list it for anyone to use.

That part worked on the first try. Within an hour of signing up, `llama-server` (the serving engine from llama.cpp, an Unsloth-maintained build on CUDA 12) was running the model on a rented machine on the other side of the world, and my coding tools were talking to it over a plain OpenAI-compatible API. Easy.

The hard, interesting part came after: making it fast enough and long-memoried enough to be genuinely pleasant to use. That's the part worth writing down, with the actual numbers.

## The slow way a model normally talks

Most people don't realize how these models generate text: one piece at a time, and checking each piece is almost as slow as writing a whole sentence. The model writes a word, stops, fully re-examines everything it's written so far to decide what comes next, writes another word, stops again. Every single word pays the full cost of that pause.

There's a shortcut called **speculative decoding**. Let the model guess several words ahead cheaply, using a shortcut built into the same model, then check all of those guesses in a single pass instead of one pass per word. If the guesses were right, which they usually are, you just got several words for close to the price of one. If a guess was wrong partway through, you redo from that point. You never end up worse off than the slow way, and most of the time you end up a lot better off.

<text x="569.4" y="424" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Inter, ui-sans-serif, system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="400" fill="#62685f">2 words kept, redo from the miss</text></g>
<g class="stageCaption"><text x="390" y="450" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Inter, ui-sans-serif, system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="600" fill="#232821">either way: never slower than checking one word at a time</text><text x="390" y="472" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Inter, ui-sans-serif, system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="11.5" font-weight="400" fill="#62685f">a wrong guess costs a small redo, never a wrong answer</text></g>
</svg>
<figcaption>Draft cheap, verify once, keep what's right.</figcaption>
</figure>

Turning this on took one flag at launch: `--spec-type draft-mtp`. The model already knew how to guess its own next few words, that ability (multi-token prediction) was baked into the GGUF, so llama.cpp just had to be told to use it, no separate draft model to download or manage. The first time I measured it, throughput went from about 12 tokens a second to about 42, close to 3.5 times faster, with no loss in quality: every guess still gets checked against the full model before it counts, so a wrong guess costs a small redo, never a wrong answer.

## Giving it a longer memory

Speed solved, the second problem was memory, specifically the model's working memory of the conversation (its **KV cache**), not RAM in the everyday sense. Everything said to it so far in a session has to stay resident on the same GPU as the model itself. Once the card fills up, the conversation can't get any longer.

At `-c 163840` (163,840 tokens of context) and full precision, the server used 30,178 MiB of the card's 32,768 MiB, leaving about 2.6 GB of headroom. That's a long conversation already, but my coding tools paste in a lot of surrounding code on every turn, and I wanted more room before hitting the wall.

The fix was **KV cache quantization**: two flags, `-ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0`, storing each cached word at 8-bit precision instead of 16-bit. At the same 163,840-token context, memory use dropped to 25,960 MiB, a 4.2 GB reduction, enough headroom to push the context all the way to 262,144 tokens, the model's full native length, while still using only 30,176 MiB. I checked this wasn't a free lunch with a catch: I sent the model the exact same prompt at `temperature: 0` (its single most confident, deterministic setting) before and after enabling the quantized cache. Both runs accepted exactly 203 of 288 speculative-decoding guesses, and produced word-for-word identical output. Throughput was unchanged too, 53 to 54 tokens a second either way. A hybrid state-space and attention model like this one only keeps a KV cache for its attention layers, which may be why it tolerates this kind of compression better than a pure attention model would.

## A trick that didn't travel

Here's the part I almost skipped writing about, because it's a story about something not working, but it taught me the most useful lesson of the project.

While researching speculative decoding, I found a published benchmark running this exact model on a Jetson Thor board, where raising `--spec-draft-n-max` (how many tokens ahead the model is allowed to guess per batch, default 3) had taken throughput from about 13 tokens a second to about 35. Free extra speed, same model: I copied the setting.

On the V100, it didn't transfer. I benchmarked each value with the same deterministic prompt, `temperature: 0`, 300 tokens, three clean server restarts:

| `--spec-draft-n-max` | tokens/second | guesses accepted |
|---|---|---|
| 3 (default) | 53.9 to 54.6 | 203 of 288 (70.5%) |
| 4 | 55.0 | 216 of 330 (65.5%) |
| 6 | 47.1 | 227 of 429 (52.9%) |

Four was a wash, inside the run-to-run noise. Six was worse: the model proposed more tokens per batch, but the acceptance rate dropped faster than the batch size grew, so each batch did more wasted work for the same payoff. The Jetson result was real, just specific to that hardware's balance of compute and memory bandwidth, which doesn't carry over to a V100. A tuning number that's a free win on one card can be a net loss on another, and the only way to know is to measure on the card you actually have.

## The sweet spot, if you're running this on a V100

If you've got this same model on the same class of card, a 32 GB V100, here's the configuration I landed on after all of the above:

```
llama-server \
  --model Qwen3.8-27B-Uncensored-Q5_K_M.gguf \
  --spec-type draft-mtp \
  -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 \
  -c 262144 \
  -ngl 999 -np 1 -b 512 -ub 512 \
  --flash-attn auto --context-shift --keep 4
```

- **`--spec-type draft-mtp`** at the default `--spec-draft-n-max` (3). Don't raise it on a V100. It doesn't help, and past 4 it actively hurts.
- **`-ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0`** always on. Measured lossless at `temperature: 0`, and it's the one change that buys real headroom.
- **`-c 262144`**, the model's full native context, only reachable because of the quantized cache. Expect roughly 30.2 GB used out of 32 GB, about 2.6 GB of margin.
- **`--context-shift`** is in the command above, but on this model it never actually engages. The server logs "KV cache shifting is not supported for this context, disabling KV cache shifting" every time. Budget for a hard wall at 262,144 tokens, not a graceful rollover past it.

Expect somewhere around 54 tokens a second on a single stream, and full native context, on a GPU you're renting by the hour rather than depreciating in a closet. None of this required new hardware or new code, just a weekend of changing one setting at a time and trusting the measurement over the write-up, including this one.
